title: Suthida
text:
Suthida Tidjai, known formally as Queen Suthida of Thailand, was born on June 3, 1978, in Hat Yai, Songkhla Province, in southern Thailand. She was the third of four children in a middle-class family, with her father, Kham Tidjai, working as a salesman and her mother, Jangheang Tidjai, as a housewife. Her early education took place at the Anuban Hat Yai School, a local primary institution, before she moved to Bangkok to attend the prestigious Rajini School, a well-known all-girls secondary school. After completing her secondary education, she enrolled at Assumption University, one of Thailand’s leading private universities, where she studied communication arts, graduating in 2000.

Following her graduation, Suthida began her career in the airline industry, joining Thai Airways International in 2000 as a flight attendant. She worked in this role for several years, gaining experience in customer service and aviation protocols. Her career took a significant turn in 2008 when she transitioned to a position in the security detail of the Bureau of the Royal Household, specifically assigned to protect then-Crown Prince Maha Vajiralongkorn. This role marked the beginning of her deeper involvement with the Thai monarchy, though details of her duties and interactions during this period remained largely private.

Suthida’s relationship with King Vajiralongkorn developed over time, and in 2014, she was appointed commander of his personal security unit, a position that elevated her status within the royal household. By this point, she had become a trusted figure, often accompanying the king at official events. On May 1, 2019, just days before his coronation, King Vajiralongkorn officially married Suthida in a private ceremony at the Amphorn Sathan Residential Hall in Bangkok’s Dusit Palace. The marriage was later announced in the *Royal Gazette*, and she was granted the title of Queen Suthida, making her the first queen consort of Thailand in nearly seven decades since Queen Sirikit, who had held the title since 1950.

As queen, Suthida assumed a prominent role in royal duties, often appearing alongside the king at state functions, religious ceremonies, and public engagements. She played a key part in the coronation ceremonies held from May 4 to 6, 2019, where she was formally anointed and presented with the royal regalia. Her public appearances increased significantly, and she became known for her composed demeanor and dedication to charitable causes. She supported initiatives in education, healthcare, and disaster relief, including donations to hospitals and schools, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021.

Queen Suthida also took on ceremonial responsibilities, such as presiding over the annual Royal Ploughing Ceremony in 2022, a traditional event symbolizing the start of the rice-growing season. She has been active in promoting Thai culture and heritage, often visiting temples and participating in Buddhist rituals. In 2020, she was appointed deputy commander-in-chief of the King’s Royal Guard, a military unit under the direct command of the monarch, further solidifying her role in both royal and military spheres.

Despite her public role, Queen Suthida has maintained a relatively low profile compared to other members of the Thai royal family. She has no children of her own but has been a stepmother to King Vajiralongkorn’s children from previous marriages. Her later life has been marked by continued involvement in royal duties, with a focus on social welfare and national unity. She remains a central figure in Thailand’s monarchy, respected for her discipline and commitment to her role, though her personal life and opinions remain closely guarded by the palace. As of 2024, she continues to serve as queen consort, fulfilling her responsibilities with the same dedication that has characterized her career since joining the royal household.

title: Fernando da Costa Novaes
text:
Fernando da Costa Novaes was a prominent Brazilian ornithologist and conservationist, born on March 1, 1927, in Belém, Pará, Brazil. He was the son of Francisco da Costa Novaes and Maria José da Costa Novaes, both of whom were of Portuguese descent. From an early age, Novaes displayed a keen interest in nature, particularly birds, influenced by the rich biodiversity of the Amazon region where he grew up. His formal education began at the Colégio Moderno in Belém, where he completed his primary and secondary studies before enrolling at the Universidade Federal do Pará (UFPA) in 1945 to study natural history.

Novaes graduated from UFPA in 1949 with a degree in natural sciences, specializing in zoology. His academic performance earned him a scholarship to pursue further studies abroad, and in 1950, he moved to the United States to attend the University of Michigan. There, he worked under the guidance of renowned ornithologist Dr. Josselyn Van Tyne, completing his Master of Science in 1952 with a thesis on the birds of the Amazon basin. His research during this period focused on the taxonomy and distribution of Neotropical bird species, laying the foundation for his future contributions to the field.

After returning to Brazil in 1953, Novaes joined the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi (MPEG) in Belém, one of the oldest and most respected scientific institutions in the Amazon. He began as an assistant researcher and quickly rose through the ranks, becoming the head of the ornithology department in 1955. During his tenure at MPEG, Novaes conducted extensive fieldwork across the Amazon, documenting bird species and their habitats. Between 1955 and 1970, he led or participated in over 30 expeditions, collecting more than 12,000 bird specimens, many of which were new to science. His work significantly expanded the museum’s ornithological collection, which grew to include over 50,000 specimens by the time of his retirement.

Novaes’s most notable scientific contributions include the description of several new bird species and subspecies, such as the *Pyrrhura amazonum* (Santarem parakeet) in 1978 and the *Myrmotherula klagesi* (Klages’s antwren) in 1990, the latter named in honor of his colleague Samuel M. Klages. He also co-authored the seminal *Ornitologia Brasileira: Uma Introdução* (1978) with Helmut Sick, a foundational text for Brazilian ornithology. His research was published in over 150 scientific papers, many in prestigious journals such as *The Auk*, *The Condor*, and *Revista Brasileira de Zoologia*. Novaes was also a dedicated educator, mentoring generations of Brazilian ornithologists and supervising numerous graduate students at UFPA and other institutions.

In addition to his scientific work, Novaes was a passionate advocate for Amazon conservation. In the 1970s and 1980s, he collaborated with international organizations such as the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) to promote the protection of the Amazon’s biodiversity. He played a key role in the establishment of several protected areas, including the Tapajós National Forest (created in 1974) and the Amazônia National Park (1974), both of which cover vast tracts of pristine rainforest. His efforts earned him recognition as one of Brazil’s leading conservationists, and in 1985, he was awarded the prestigious Prêmio Almirante Álvaro Alberto by the Brazilian National Council for Scientific and Technological Development (CNPq).

Novaes retired from MPEG in 1992 but remained active in ornithology and conservation. He continued to publish research and advise younger scientists until his health declined in the early 2000s. In his later years, he lived in Belém, where he was frequently consulted by researchers and journalists on matters related to Amazonian biodiversity. Fernando da Costa Novaes passed away on November 15, 2004, at the age of 77, due to complications from a stroke. His legacy endures through the countless species he described, the students he mentored, and the protected areas he helped establish, ensuring that his contributions to science and conservation will be remembered for generations.

title: Jan Zamoyski
text:
Jan Zamoyski was born on March 19, 1542, in Skokówka, a village in the Lublin Voivodeship of the Kingdom of Poland, into the influential Zamoyski noble family. His father, Stanisław Zamoyski, was a castellan of Chełm, and his mother, Anna Herburt, came from a prominent Ruthenian family. From an early age, Jan displayed exceptional intellectual abilities, which led his parents to provide him with a rigorous education. At the age of 13, in 1555, he was sent to study at the University of Paris, where he spent six years mastering classical languages, philosophy, and law. He later continued his studies at the University of Strasbourg and the University of Padua, earning a doctorate in law in 1561 at the age of 19.

Upon returning to Poland in 1563, Zamoyski entered the royal court of King Sigismund II Augustus, where his legal expertise and diplomatic skills quickly earned him recognition. In 1565, he was appointed secretary to the king, and by 1566, he became a royal referendary, a position that involved advising the monarch on legal and administrative matters. His rise continued when, in 1571, he was named Crown Chancellor, a role that placed him at the center of Poland’s political and legal affairs. During this period, he played a key role in drafting the *Henrician Articles* (1573), a constitutional document that established the elective monarchy in Poland and limited the power of the king, ensuring the nobility’s rights.

Zamoyski’s political career reached its peak during the reign of King Stephen Báthory (1576–1586), whom he had supported in the 1575 royal election. As Crown Chancellor and Grand Hetman of the Crown (a military title he received in 1581), Zamoyski became one of the most powerful figures in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. He was instrumental in modernizing the Polish army, introducing reforms such as the establishment of a standing infantry force and improving artillery units. His military leadership was demonstrated during the Livonian War (1558–1583), where he commanded Polish forces to victory in several key battles, including the Battle of Pskov (1581–1582), which forced Ivan the Terrible to cede Livonia to Poland in the Treaty of Jam Zapolski (1582).

Beyond his military and political achievements, Zamoyski was a patron of education and culture. In 1589, he founded the Zamość Academy, a university in the newly established town of Zamość, which he had designed as an ideal Renaissance city. The academy, modeled after Western European universities, became a center of learning in Poland, offering courses in law, medicine, and the humanities. Zamość itself, built between 1579 and 1585, was a marvel of urban planning, featuring a grid layout, fortifications, and grand public buildings, many of which still stand today.

Zamoyski’s influence waned slightly after the death of Stephen Báthory in 1586, as he clashed with the new king, Sigismund III Vasa, over foreign policy and the king’s pro-Habsburg leanings. Despite their differences, Zamoyski remained a key figure in the Commonwealth. In 1588, he played a decisive role in the War of the Polish Succession, defeating the Habsburg-backed Maximilian III of Austria at the Battle of Byczyna. This victory secured Sigismund III’s throne and reinforced Poland’s position in Europe. However, Zamoyski’s opposition to Sigismund’s policies, particularly his support for the Habsburgs and his attempts to centralize power, led to his gradual marginalization.

In his later years, Zamoyski focused on managing his vast estates, which included over 11 cities and 200 villages, making him one of the wealthiest magnates in Poland. He also continued to advocate for the rights of the nobility and the preservation of the Commonwealth’s political system. Jan Zamoyski died on June 3, 1605, in Zamość, at the age of 63. He was buried in the Zamoyski family crypt in the Collegiate Church of St. Thomas in Zamość. His legacy endured through his contributions to Poland’s legal, military, and educational institutions, as well as his visionary urban planning in Zamość, which remains a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo
text:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, known as "El Jefe de Jefes" (The Boss of Bosses), was one of Mexico’s most powerful drug traffickers during the late 20th century. Born on January 8, 1946, in Bellavista, a neighborhood in Culiacán, Sinaloa, Mexico, Félix Gallardo grew up in a modest family. His early life was unremarkable, but his ambition and connections would later propel him into the upper echelons of Mexico’s criminal underworld.

Félix Gallardo began his career in law enforcement, working as a federal judicial police agent in the 1970s. This position provided him with valuable insights into the workings of the Mexican legal system and the drug trade. By the late 1970s, he had transitioned into drug trafficking, leveraging his police connections to facilitate the smuggling of marijuana and opium into the United States. His early operations were based in Sinaloa, a state with a long history of drug cultivation and trafficking.

In the early 1980s, Félix Gallardo played a pivotal role in the formation of the Guadalajara Cartel, one of Mexico’s first major drug trafficking organizations. Alongside Rafael Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, he established a powerful syndicate that controlled the flow of drugs from Mexico into the U.S. The cartel’s operations expanded rapidly, with Félix Gallardo overseeing the trafficking of cocaine, marijuana, and heroin. By 1984, the Guadalajara Cartel was responsible for smuggling an estimated 2,000 kilograms of cocaine per month into the United States, generating hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue.

Félix Gallardo’s influence extended beyond drug trafficking. He cultivated relationships with Mexican politicians, law enforcement officials, and business leaders, ensuring protection for his operations. His ability to corrupt and manipulate the system earned him the nickname "El Jefe de Jefes." One of his most notable achievements was the establishment of a sophisticated smuggling network that included airstrips, warehouses, and distribution routes across Mexico and the U.S.

However, Félix Gallardo’s reign began to unravel in 1985 following the kidnapping, torture, and murder of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena. Camarena, who had been investigating the Guadalajara Cartel, was abducted on February 7, 1985, in Guadalajara, Jalisco. His body was found a month later in a rural area of Michoacán. The murder sparked a massive international investigation, leading to increased pressure on the Mexican government to dismantle the cartel.

In response to the Camarena case, Félix Gallardo attempted to reorganize his operations to evade law enforcement. In 1987, he convened a meeting in Acapulco with key lieutenants, including Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán, Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, and the Arellano Félix brothers. At this meeting, Félix Gallardo divided the cartel’s territories among his associates, effectively fragmenting the Guadalajara Cartel into smaller, regional organizations. This move was intended to reduce the risk of detection and prosecution, but it also marked the beginning of a new era of cartel violence in Mexico.

Despite his efforts to maintain control, Félix Gallardo’s downfall was inevitable. On April 8, 1989, he was arrested in Guadalajara by Mexican authorities. His arrest was the result of a joint operation between Mexican and U.S. law enforcement agencies. Félix Gallardo was charged with the murder of Enrique Camarena, drug trafficking, and organized crime. In 1990, he was convicted and sentenced to 40 years in prison.

During his incarceration, Félix Gallardo continued to exert influence over Mexico’s drug trade, communicating with his associates through intermediaries. However, his power waned as rival cartels, such as the Sinaloa Cartel and the Tijuana Cartel, gained prominence. In 2017, Félix Gallardo was transferred from a maximum-security prison to a medium-security facility due to health issues, including hearing loss and partial blindness. As of 2024, he remains incarcerated, serving his sentence in Mexico.

Félix Gallardo’s legacy is a complex one. He is often credited with laying the foundation for modern Mexican drug trafficking organizations, transforming a fragmented industry into a highly organized and lucrative enterprise. His ability to navigate the political and criminal landscapes of Mexico made him one of the most influential figures in the history of the country’s drug trade. Despite his imprisonment, his impact on Mexico’s criminal underworld continues to be felt.

title: Iggy Azalea
text:
Iggy Azalea, born Amethyst Amelia Kelly on June 7, 1990, in Sydney, Australia, is a rapper, singer, and model who rose to international fame in the early 2010s. She grew up in Mullumbimby, a small town in New South Wales, where her father, Brendan Kelly, was a painter and comic artist, and her mother, Tanya Kelly, worked as a cleaner and hotel maid. Azalea was the middle child of three siblings, with an older sister and a younger brother. From a young age, she developed an interest in hip-hop, particularly artists like Tupac Shakur and Missy Elliott, which influenced her decision to pursue a career in music.

At the age of 14, Azalea formed a girl group with two friends, inspired by the Spice Girls, but the group disbanded after a year. Determined to pursue music seriously, she dropped out of high school at 16 and moved to the United States to chase her dreams. She initially settled in Miami, Florida, before relocating to Houston, Texas, where she lived with her mother for a short time. In 2009, she moved to Atlanta, Georgia, a hub for Southern hip-hop, to further her career. It was during this time that she adopted the stage name "Iggy Azalea," combining her dog’s name, Iggy, with the street she grew up on, Azalea Street.

Azalea’s breakthrough came in 2011 when she released her debut mixtape, *Ignorant Art*, on September 27. The project featured tracks like "Pu$$y" and "My World," which showcased her bold, confident style and Southern hip-hop influences. The mixtape gained attention online, and she quickly built a following on social media. In 2012, she released two free EPs, *Glory* and *TrapGold*, the latter of which included the track "Fancy," though it was a different version from the one that would later become her biggest hit. That same year, she signed a record deal with Grand Hustle Records, owned by rapper T.I., who became her mentor.

Her commercial success came in 2014 with the release of her debut studio album, *The New Classic*, on April 21. The album debuted at number 3 on the *Billboard* 200 and was certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). It included the hit singles "Fancy," featuring Charli XCX, which peaked at number 1 on the *Billboard* Hot 100 for seven consecutive weeks, and "Problem" with Ariana Grande, which reached number 2. "Fancy" also topped charts in Canada, the UK, and Australia, making Azalea the first non-American female rapper to achieve a number-one single on the *Billboard* Hot 100. The album earned her two Grammy Award nominations in 2015 for Best New Artist and Best Rap Album.

Despite her rapid rise, Azalea faced criticism for her cultural appropriation and perceived lack of authenticity in hip-hop, particularly as a white Australian rapper adopting African American Vernacular English (AAVE) and Southern hip-hop aesthetics. She also faced backlash for controversial tweets and public statements, including feuds with other artists like Azealia Banks and Nicki Minaj. In 2015, she released the single "Team," which underperformed compared to her previous hits, signaling a decline in her commercial momentum.

Azalea’s second studio album, *Digital Distortion*, was initially set for release in 2016 but was ultimately shelved due to creative differences with her label and personal struggles. She left Grand Hustle Records in 2017 and later signed with Island Records. In 2018, she released the EP *Survive the Summer*, which included the single "Kream" featuring Tyga. The EP debuted at number 144 on the *Billboard* 200, a significant drop from her previous work. In 2019, she released her second studio album, *In My Defense*, independently through her own label, Bad Dreams Records, followed by *The End of an Era* in 2021, which also failed to replicate her earlier success.

Outside of music, Azalea has ventured into modeling and business. In 2014, she became a face of Forever 21 and later collaborated with Steve Madden on a shoe line. She also launched a makeup line, "Savage X Fenty," in partnership with Rihanna’s lingerie brand in 2019. In 2020, she gave birth to her first child, a son named Onyx Kelly, with her then-partner, rapper Playboi Carti. The couple’s relationship ended shortly after, and Azalea has since kept her personal life largely private.

Despite the controversies and commercial fluctuations, Iggy Azalea remains a notable figure in hip-hop, known for her early impact on the genre and her role in bringing female rap to mainstream audiences. As of 2024, she continues to release music independently and engage with her fanbase through social media, though her career has not regained the same level of prominence it held during its peak in the mid-2010s.

title: Radhika Apte
text:
Radhika Apte was born on September 7, 1985, in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, India, into a Marathi family with roots in Maharashtra. Her father, Dr. Charudutt Apte, was a neurosurgeon, and her mother, Jayashree Apte, worked as a gynecologist. Due to her parents' professions, the family frequently relocated during her childhood, living in cities like Pune, Mumbai, and Delhi. Radhika spent a significant part of her early years in Pune, where she attended the Daffodils English School. She later enrolled at Fergusson College, also in Pune, where she pursued a degree in economics and mathematics, graduating in 2005.

Apte’s interest in acting developed early, influenced by her exposure to theater during her school and college years. In 2005, shortly after graduating, she moved to Mumbai to pursue a career in acting. She joined the theater group "Arpana," founded by theater director Sunil Shanbag, where she honed her skills in stage performances. Her first professional acting role came in 2005 with the Bengali film *Antaheen*, directed by Aniruddha Roy Chowdhury, though her scenes were eventually cut from the final version. Undeterred, she continued working in theater and independent films, making her official film debut in 2009 with the Hindi film *Vaah! Life Ho Toh Aisi!*, directed by Mahesh Manjrekar. The same year, she appeared in the Marathi film *Gho Mala Asla Hava*, directed by Sumitra Bhave and Sunil Sukthankar, which earned her critical recognition.

The early 2010s marked a turning point in Apte’s career as she began gaining wider attention. In 2010, she starred in the Tamil film *Rakta Charitra*, directed by Ram Gopal Varma, which was a commercial success. Her performance in the 2011 Marathi film *Ha Bharat Maza*, directed by Sumitra Bhave and Sunil Sukthankar, further established her as a versatile actress. However, it was her role in the 2015 Hindi film *Badlapur*, directed by Sriram Raghavan, that brought her mainstream recognition. Her portrayal of a grieving mother earned praise, and the film grossed over ₹75 crore (approximately $11 million) at the box office. That same year, she appeared in the critically acclaimed independent film *Hunterrr*, directed by Harshavardhan Kulkarni, which showcased her ability to handle bold and unconventional roles.

Apte’s career reached new heights in 2016 when she starred in three Netflix original productions: *Sacred Games*, *Ghoul*, and *Lust Stories*. *Sacred Games*, directed by Anurag Kashyap and Vikramaditya Motwane, became one of Netflix’s most-watched Indian series, with Apte playing the role of Anjali Mathur, a RAW agent. *Ghoul*, a horror miniseries directed by Patrick Graham, and *Lust Stories*, an anthology film directed by Anurag Kashyap, Zoya Akhtar, Dibakar Banerjee, and Karan Johar, further cemented her reputation as a bold and fearless performer. Her performance in *Lust Stories* earned her a nomination for the International Emmy Award for Best Actress in 2019, making her the first Indian actress to receive such a nomination.

In 2018, Apte starred in the Hindi film *Pad Man*, directed by R. Balki, alongside Akshay Kumar and Sonam Kapoor. The film, based on the true story of Arunachalam Muruganantham, a social activist who revolutionized menstrual hygiene in rural India, was a commercial success, grossing over ₹207 crore (approximately $30 million) worldwide. That same year, she appeared in the Hollywood film *The Wedding Guest*, directed by Michael Winterbottom, marking her international debut. Her performance in the film, alongside Dev Patel, was well-received, though the film had a limited release.

Apte continued to work in both Indian and international projects in the following years. In 2020, she starred in the Hindi film *Bamfaad*, directed by Ranjan Chandel, and the Marathi film *Bai*, directed by Vijay Patkar. She also appeared in the Netflix series *OK Computer*, directed by Pooja Shetty and Neil Pagedar, which premiered in 2021. In 2022, she starred in the Hindi film *Monica, O My Darling*, directed by Vasan Bala, which premiered on Netflix and received positive reviews for its quirky storytelling and Apte’s performance. The same year, she made her debut in the Telugu film industry with *F3: Fun and Frustration*, directed by Anil Ravipudi, which was a box office success.

Beyond acting, Apte has been vocal about issues such as gender equality, mental health, and the challenges faced by women in the film industry. She married British musician Benedict Taylor in 2012, and the couple has maintained a private personal life, rarely discussing their relationship in public. Apte has also been involved in various philanthropic activities, including supporting education for underprivileged children and advocating for animal rights.

As of 2024, Radhika Apte remains one of India’s most versatile and internationally recognized actresses, known for her willingness to take on challenging roles across languages and genres. Her filmography includes over 50 films and web series, spanning Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Bengali, and English languages. With numerous awards and nominations to her credit, including Filmfare Awards, Screen Awards, and the aforementioned International Emmy nomination, she continues to be a prominent figure in Indian cinema.

title: David Galloway (writer)
text:
David Galloway was born on August 12, 1937, in Memphis, Tennessee, to James Galloway, a schoolteacher, and Margaret Galloway (née Thompson), a homemaker. Raised in a middle-class household, he developed an early interest in literature, influenced by his father’s extensive personal library. After graduating from Central High School in Memphis in 1955, he enrolled at Vanderbilt University, where he studied English literature under the mentorship of poet and critic Donald Davidson. Galloway earned his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1959, graduating *magna cum laude*, and went on to pursue a Master of Arts at the University of Chicago, completing his thesis on the works of William Faulkner in 1961.

Galloway’s academic career began in 1962 when he accepted a teaching position at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon, where he taught English literature for three years. During this time, he immersed himself in Middle Eastern culture and began writing essays on contemporary Arab literature, contributing to journals such as *The Middle East Journal* and *Encounter*. His first major publication, *The Absurd Hero in American Fiction: Updike, Styron, Bellow, Salinger* (1966), emerged from his doctoral research at the University of Freiburg in West Germany, where he earned his Ph.D. in comparative literature in 1965. The book, which analyzed the existential themes in post-war American fiction, was praised for its insightful critique and established Galloway as a serious literary scholar.

In 1967, Galloway returned to the United States to take a position as an assistant professor of English at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio. He remained at the university for over three decades, eventually becoming a full professor in 1978. During his tenure, he published extensively on American and European literature, including *The Other Writing: Postmodern Poetics and the Novel* (1987), which examined the experimental techniques of writers like Thomas Pynchon and Italo Calvino. He also edited *The Norton Anthology of Short Fiction* (1978), a widely adopted textbook that went through multiple editions, selling over 500,000 copies by the time of his retirement.

Beyond academia, Galloway was an active literary critic and essayist, contributing reviews to *The New York Times Book Review*, *The Times Literary Supplement*, and *The Washington Post*. His essays often explored the intersections of literature and philosophy, particularly the works of existentialist and postmodern writers. In 1992, he received a Fulbright Scholarship to teach at the University of Warsaw in Poland, where he lectured on American literature and conducted research on Eastern European literary responses to totalitarianism. His experiences in Poland later informed his book *Voices from the Iron Curtain: Literature and Resistance in Cold War Europe* (1996), which was shortlisted for the National Book Critics Circle Award in criticism.

Galloway’s later career was marked by a shift toward creative writing. In 2001, he published his first novel, *The Last of the True Believers*, a semi-autobiographical work set in 1960s Beirut, which received favorable reviews for its vivid portrayal of expatriate life in the Middle East. His second novel, *The Professor’s Daughter* (2005), explored themes of academic rivalry and personal reinvention, drawing on his decades of experience in higher education. Though not commercial bestsellers, both novels were well-regarded in literary circles and solidified his reputation as a writer of quiet, introspective fiction.

After retiring from Case Western Reserve in 2002, Galloway divided his time between Cleveland and a second home in Provence, France, where he continued to write and travel. He remained an occasional contributor to literary journals and gave guest lectures at universities, including a 2010 visiting professorship at the University of Edinburgh. In his later years, he suffered from Parkinson’s disease, which gradually limited his mobility, though he remained intellectually active until his death. David Galloway passed away on November 3, 2021, at the age of 84, in Cleveland, Ohio. He was survived by his wife of 52 years, Eleanor Galloway (née Whitmore), a former librarian, and their two children, James and Claire. His papers, including manuscripts and correspondence, were donated to the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Columbia University.

title: Cheyenne Brando
text:
Cheyenne Brando was born on February 20, 1970, in Tahiti, French Polynesia, to legendary actor Marlon Brando and his third wife, Tarita Teriipaia, a Tahitian actress. She was the youngest of Marlon Brando’s eleven children, though only three—Christian, Miko, and Cheyenne—were officially recognized by him. Her birth name was Tarita Cheyenne Brando, but she was commonly known as Cheyenne. Growing up in Tahiti, she spent much of her early childhood on the family’s private island, Tetiaroa, a 5.5-square-mile atoll that Marlon Brando purchased in 1966. The island provided a secluded upbringing, though her parents’ marriage was tumultuous, and they divorced in 1972 when Cheyenne was just two years old.

Cheyenne’s early life was marked by instability. Her father, though famous, was often absent, and her mother struggled with mental health issues, including depression. Despite this, Cheyenne was close to her half-brother Christian Brando, who was 16 years her senior. In 1989, at the age of 19, she moved to Los Angeles to live with Christian, hoping to pursue a career in modeling or acting. However, her time in California was short-lived and fraught with difficulties. She had little professional success in the entertainment industry, though she briefly appeared in a few minor roles, including a small part in the 1991 film *The Freshman*, which starred her father.

Tragedy struck Cheyenne’s life on May 16, 1990, when her fiancé, Dag Drollet, a Tahitian surfer and model, was shot and killed in a confrontation with her half-brother Christian. The incident occurred at the Brando family home in Beverly Hills. Christian, who had a history of violent behavior and substance abuse, claimed the shooting was accidental, but he was charged with first-degree murder. The case drew intense media scrutiny, and Cheyenne, who was pregnant with Drollet’s child, became a central figure in the trial. She testified against Christian, describing the events leading up to the shooting, though her testimony was inconsistent due to her emotional state and possible substance use. Christian was ultimately convicted of voluntary manslaughter and sentenced to ten years in prison, serving five before his release in 1996.

Cheyenne gave birth to her son, Tuki Brando, on July 27, 1990, just over two months after Drollet’s death. The birth was difficult, and Cheyenne struggled with severe depression in the aftermath of the tragedy. She returned to Tahiti shortly after the trial, where she attempted to rebuild her life. However, her mental health continued to deteriorate, exacerbated by the loss of her fiancé and the strain of the trial. She made several suicide attempts in the early 1990s, including an overdose in 1991 that required hospitalization.

In 1995, Cheyenne’s life took another tragic turn when she was involved in a serious car accident in Tahiti. She suffered severe injuries, including a broken jaw and facial fractures, which required multiple surgeries. The accident left her with lasting physical and emotional scars. Despite these challenges, she remained close to her son, Tuki, who later became a model and actor, following in the footsteps of his famous family.

Cheyenne’s relationship with her father, Marlon Brando, was complicated. Though he provided financial support, he was often distant, and their interactions were limited. In his later years, Marlon Brando expressed regret over his absentee parenting, though he made few efforts to reconnect with Cheyenne. She reportedly resented his lack of involvement in her life, particularly during her most difficult periods.

On April 16, 1995, Cheyenne Brando died by suicide in Punaauia, Tahiti, at the age of 25. She hanged herself in her mother’s home, leaving behind her five-year-old son, Tuki. Her death was a devastating conclusion to a life marked by trauma, loss, and unfulfilled potential. In the years following her death, her story has been revisited in documentaries and biographies about the Brando family, often highlighting the destructive legacy of fame, neglect, and mental illness. Tuki Brando, who was raised by his grandmother Tarita, has spoken publicly about his mother’s struggles, preserving her memory while forging his own path.

title: Braulio Lara
text:
Braulio Lara was born on December 20, 1988, in Baní, Peravia Province, Dominican Republic. From a young age, he showed a natural talent for baseball, a sport deeply embedded in Dominican culture. Growing up in Baní, a town known for producing Major League Baseball (MLB) talent, Lara was influenced by the success of local players who had made it to the big leagues. His early years were spent playing in local youth leagues, where his pitching skills quickly set him apart.

Lara’s professional career began when he signed with the Los Angeles Dodgers as an international free agent on July 2, 2007, at the age of 18. The Dodgers scouting department, impressed by his fastball and developing secondary pitches, saw potential in the young left-handed pitcher. He was assigned to the Dominican Summer League (DSL) Dodgers, where he made his professional debut in 2008. That season, he appeared in 14 games, posting a 3-3 record with a 2.63 earned run average (ERA) and 53 strikeouts in 51.1 innings pitched. His performance earned him a promotion to the Gulf Coast League (GCL) Dodgers in 2009, where he continued to refine his skills, recording a 2.89 ERA in 10 appearances.

In 2010, Lara was assigned to the Ogden Raptors, the Dodgers’ rookie-level affiliate in the Pioneer League. He had a breakout season, going 6-1 with a 2.36 ERA and 78 strikeouts in 68.1 innings, which caught the attention of the organization. His progress continued in 2011 with the Great Lakes Loons, the Dodgers’ Class A affiliate in the Midwest League, where he posted a 4-5 record with a 3.86 ERA in 23 starts. Despite some inconsistency, his fastball velocity, which sat in the low 90s, and his improving curveball made him a prospect to watch.

Lara’s career took a significant turn on July 31, 2012, when he was traded to the Tampa Bay Rays as part of a three-team deal that sent infielder Ryan Roberts to the Arizona Diamondbacks. The Rays assigned him to their High-A affiliate, the Charlotte Stone Crabs, where he finished the 2012 season with a 2.57 ERA in six starts. In 2013, he split time between Charlotte and the Double-A Montgomery Biscuits, compiling a combined 4-5 record with a 3.58 ERA in 26 appearances (16 starts). His performance earned him a spot on the Rays’ 40-man roster after the season.

Lara made his MLB debut on April 2, 2014, against the Toronto Blue Jays at Rogers Centre. He pitched 1.1 innings, allowing one run on two hits while striking out one. However, his time in the majors was short-lived; he appeared in only three games that season, posting a 6.75 ERA before being optioned back to the minors. He spent the remainder of 2014 with the Triple-A Durham Bulls, where he struggled with a 5.30 ERA in 26 appearances.

In 2015, Lara was designated for assignment by the Rays on April 4 and claimed off waivers by the Miami Marlins the following day. He spent the season with the Triple-A New Orleans Zephyrs, where he had a 4-4 record with a 4.32 ERA in 43 relief appearances. His time with the Marlins organization was brief, as he was released on March 30, 2016. Lara then signed a minor league contract with the Chicago White Sox on April 15, 2016, but was released in June after struggling in the minors.

After his release, Lara returned to the Dominican Republic, where he played for the Tigres del Licey in the Dominican Winter League during the 2016-2017 season. He appeared in 11 games, posting a 2.70 ERA in 13.1 innings. Despite his efforts, he did not receive another MLB opportunity. In 2017, he signed with the Vaqueros Unión Laguna of the Mexican League, where he had a 5.40 ERA in 11 appearances before being released.

Lara’s later years were spent playing in independent leagues and winter ball. In 2018, he signed with the Lancaster Barnstormers of the Atlantic League, where he appeared in 20 games, posting a 3.60 ERA. He also played for the Algodoneros de Unión Laguna in the Mexican League that year, though his performance was inconsistent. His final professional season came in 2019, when he played for the Tigres del Licey in the Dominican Winter League, appearing in four games with a 4.50 ERA.

After retiring from professional baseball, Lara remained involved in the sport in the Dominican Republic, occasionally working with young pitchers in his hometown of Baní. He also became a coach for local youth teams, sharing his knowledge and experience with the next generation of players. Despite not achieving sustained success in the majors, Lara’s career spanned over a decade, during which he played at various levels of professional baseball in multiple countries. His journey reflected the challenges and unpredictability of a baseball career, particularly for international players. Lara passed away on July 20, 2022, at the age of 33, due to complications from a sudden illness. His death was mourned by fans and former teammates in the Dominican Republic and beyond.

title: Katherine Ryan
text:
Katherine Ryan was born on June 30, 1983, in Sarnia, Ontario, Canada, to an Irish-Canadian family. Her father, Finbarr Ryan, was an engineer, and her mother, Julie Ryan, worked in education. She grew up in a household of six children, with three brothers and two sisters, in the small industrial city of Sarnia, which is located near the border with the United States. Ryan attended St. Patrick’s High School in Sarnia, where she was known for her sharp wit and outgoing personality. After graduating in 2001, she moved to Toronto to study city planning at the University of Toronto, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in 2005.

Ryan’s early career was not in comedy but in the corporate world. After university, she worked as a corporate trainer for Hooters, the American restaurant chain known for its wings and waitstaff uniforms. She spent several years traveling across North America, training employees in customer service and operations. During this time, she also began performing stand-up comedy in Toronto’s open mic scene, making her first appearances in 2006. Her early sets were often self-deprecating, drawing on her experiences as a young woman navigating dating, work, and family life.

By 2008, Ryan had decided to pursue comedy full-time, relocating to London, England, a city she had visited briefly and felt drawn to for its vibrant comedy scene. She quickly established herself in the UK, performing at clubs like The Comedy Store and The Stand, and making her television debut in 2010 on the Channel 4 show *Stand Up for the Week*. Her sharp, confident style—often addressing themes of feminism, relationships, and her Canadian-Irish identity—resonated with audiences. That same year, she appeared on *Mock the Week*, a popular panel show, marking her first of many appearances on British television.

Ryan’s breakthrough came in 2012 when she was named Best Newcomer at the Leicester Comedy Festival, one of the UK’s most prestigious comedy awards. That year, she also released her first stand-up special, *Katherine Ryan: The Sextape*, which was filmed at the Soho Theatre in London. The special showcased her signature blend of observational humor and personal storytelling, covering topics like modern dating, body image, and cultural differences between Canada and the UK. By this time, she was a regular on panel shows, including *8 Out of 10 Cats*, *QI*, and *Have I Got News for You*, where her quick wit and unapologetic humor made her a standout performer.

In 2015, Ryan expanded her career into hosting, taking over as the presenter of *Hair*, a reality competition show on BBC Three. The show, which ran for one series, featured contestants competing in hairdressing challenges. Though short-lived, it demonstrated her versatility. That same year, she released her second stand-up special, *Katherine Ryan: In Trouble*, which premiered on Netflix in 2017. The special was filmed at the Hammersmith Apollo in London and further cemented her reputation as one of the UK’s leading comedians. She also began making inroads in the United States, performing at festivals like Just for Laughs in Montreal and appearing on *The Late Late Show with James Corden*.

Ryan’s career continued to diversify in the late 2010s. In 2018, she served as a judge on *Britain’s Got Talent*, alongside Simon Cowell, Amanda Holden, and Alesha Dixon. Her role on the show, which aired on ITV, introduced her to a broader audience and showcased her ability to balance humor with constructive criticism. That same year, she launched her podcast, *The Katherine Ryan Show*, where she interviewed guests ranging from comedians to musicians, often discussing their careers and personal lives with her trademark candor. In 2019, she released her third stand-up special, *Katherine Ryan: Glitter Room*, which premiered on Netflix and was filmed at the Eventim Apollo in London. The special explored themes of motherhood, aging, and self-acceptance, reflecting her personal journey as a single mother to her daughter, Violet, born in 2009.

Beyond comedy, Ryan has been open about her personal life, including her experiences with fertility treatments and single motherhood. She has used her platform to advocate for women’s rights and body positivity, often speaking out against societal pressures on women. In 2020, she published her first book, *The Audacity*, a collection of essays that blended humor with personal reflections on her life, career, and the challenges of being a woman in the public eye. The book was well-received, with critics praising its honesty and wit.

As of 2024, Ryan continues to perform stand-up comedy, tour internationally, and appear on television. She has maintained a strong presence in both the UK and North America, performing at venues like the O2 Arena in London and the Beacon Theatre in New York. She has also ventured into acting, appearing in the 2021 film *The Sparks Brothers*, a documentary about the American pop band Sparks, directed by Edgar Wright. Ryan’s career, marked by her fearless humor and adaptability, has made her one of the most recognizable and respected comedians of her generation. Despite her success, she remains grounded, often crediting her upbringing in Sarnia and her family for keeping her connected to her roots.

title: Matthew Perry
text:
Matthew Perry was born on August 19, 1969, in Williamstown, Massachusetts, to Suzanne Marie Morrison, a Canadian journalist and former press secretary to Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, and John Bennett Perry, an American actor. His parents divorced when he was just one year old, and he was primarily raised by his mother in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada. Perry attended Rockcliffe Park Public School and later Ashbury College, both prestigious institutions in Ottawa. From a young age, he showed an interest in acting and tennis, excelling in the latter and even considering a professional career before ultimately pursuing acting.

Perry moved to Los Angeles at the age of 15 to live with his father and attend Buckley School, a private preparatory school in Sherman Oaks, California. He began acting in high school productions and landed his first television role in 1979 at the age of 10, appearing in a single episode of the Canadian series *240-Robert*. His early career included minor roles in television shows such as *Second Chance* (1987) and *Growing Pains* (1988). In 1988, he made his film debut in *A Night in the Life of Jimmy Reardon*, though his role was small. That same year, he appeared in the short-lived sitcom *Sydney*, starring alongside Valerie Bertinelli, which was canceled after 13 episodes.

Perry’s breakthrough came in 1994 when he was cast as Chandler Bing in the NBC sitcom *Friends*, created by David Crane and Marta Kauffman. The show premiered on September 22, 1994, and quickly became a cultural phenomenon, running for 10 seasons until May 6, 2004. Perry’s portrayal of the sarcastic, self-deprecating Chandler earned him widespread acclaim and made him a household name. He received an Emmy Award nomination for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series in 2002, as well as a Golden Globe nomination in 2003. *Friends* became one of the most successful television shows in history, with Perry and his co-stars earning up to $1 million per episode in the final seasons. The show’s success also led to numerous awards, including a Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Comedy Series in 1996.

Outside of *Friends*, Perry had a mixed career in film and television. He starred in the 1997 romantic comedy *Fools Rush In* alongside Salma Hayek, which grossed over $29 million domestically. He also appeared in *The Whole Nine Yards* (2000) and its sequel, *The Whole Ten Yards* (2004), co-starring with Bruce Willis. While *The Whole Nine Yards* was a box office success, earning over $106 million worldwide, the sequel underperformed. Perry also ventured into producing, executive producing and starring in the short-lived NBC sitcom *Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip* (2006–2007), created by Aaron Sorkin. Despite critical praise, the show was canceled after one season due to low ratings.

Perry’s personal life was often marked by struggles with addiction. He first entered rehab at the age of 26 in 1997 for an addiction to prescription painkillers and alcohol. Over the years, he underwent multiple stints in rehab, including a 2001 stay at the Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation in Minnesota. In his 2022 memoir, *Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing*, Perry revealed that he had spent over $9 million on sobriety efforts and had been hospitalized 14 times, including two instances where he was placed on life support due to complications from pancreatitis. Despite these challenges, he remained sober for the last 18 months of his life.

In his later years, Perry focused on advocacy for addiction recovery. He purchased a sober living facility in Malibu, California, in 2013, which he later sold in 2018. He also became an outspoken advocate for drug court programs, testifying before the U.S. Congress in 2018 about the importance of treatment over incarceration for nonviolent drug offenders. Perry continued to act sporadically, appearing in the 2012 television movie *The Kennedys* and the 2015 sitcom *The Odd Couple*, a reboot of the classic series in which he played Oscar Madison. His final television role was in the 2021 HBO Max series *The Other Two*, where he had a recurring guest role.

On October 28, 2023, Matthew Perry was found dead in the hot tub of his home in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles. He was 54 years old. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner later ruled his death an accident, attributing it to the "acute effects of ketamine," a dissociative anesthetic that had been prescribed for depression and anxiety. Perry’s passing prompted an outpouring of tributes from fans and colleagues, celebrating his talent, humor, and resilience in the face of personal struggles. His memoir, published just a year before his death, offered an unflinching look at his battles with addiction and his journey toward sobriety, leaving behind a complex legacy as both a beloved entertainer and a symbol of the challenges of fame and recovery.

title: Mihai Eminescu
text:
Mihai Eminescu, born Mihail Eminovici on January 15, 1850, in Botoșani, Moldavia (now part of Romania), is widely regarded as Romania’s national poet and one of the most influential figures in Romanian literature. His parents, Gheorghe Eminovici, a tax collector, and Raluca Iurașcu, the daughter of a Moldavian nobleman, provided him with a modest but culturally rich upbringing. Eminescu was the seventh of eleven children, and his early education began at the primary school in Botoșani, where he studied from 1858 to 1860. He later attended the National College in Cernăuți (now Chernivtsi, Ukraine), where he excelled in languages, philosophy, and literature, graduating in 1866.

At the age of 16, Eminescu left home to join a traveling theater troupe, the *Trupa Fani Tardini-Vlădicescu*, as a prompter and occasional actor. This period, from 1866 to 1869, exposed him to the cultural and intellectual life of various Romanian regions, including Transylvania and Wallachia. In 1866, his first published poem, *"La mormântul lui Aron Pumnul"* ("At Aron Pumnul’s Grave"), appeared in the literary magazine *Familia*, marking the beginning of his literary career. The following year, he enrolled at the University of Vienna, where he studied philosophy, law, and economics from 1869 to 1872. During this time, he became deeply influenced by German Romanticism, particularly the works of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Friedrich Schiller, and Arthur Schopenhauer, as well as by Indian philosophy, which later shaped his poetic themes.

In 1872, Eminescu moved to Berlin to continue his studies at the University of Berlin, funded by a scholarship from the Romanian literary society *Junimea*. There, he attended lectures by prominent philosophers such as Friedrich Paulsen and Wilhelm Dilthey. However, financial difficulties and his growing disillusionment with academic life led him to abandon his studies in 1874. That same year, he returned to Romania and settled in Iași, where he became actively involved with *Junimea*, a conservative literary society that played a pivotal role in shaping modern Romanian literature. Eminescu worked as a librarian at the Central University Library in Iași from 1874 to 1877, a position that allowed him to immerse himself in classical and contemporary literature.

Eminescu’s literary output flourished during this period. Between 1870 and 1883, he wrote some of his most celebrated works, including the epic poem *"Luceafărul"* ("The Morning Star," 1883), which is often considered his masterpiece. Other notable works from this time include *"Scrisoarea III"* ("The Third Letter," 1881), a satirical critique of Romanian society; *"Floare albastră"* ("Blue Flower," 1873), a lyrical meditation on love and nature; and *"Doina"* (1883), a deeply emotional poem reflecting on national identity and suffering. His poetry, characterized by its philosophical depth, lyrical beauty, and exploration of themes such as love, nature, and existential despair, earned him widespread acclaim. By the late 1870s, he had become the leading figure of Romanian Romanticism and a central voice in the country’s cultural renaissance.

In addition to his poetry, Eminescu was a prolific journalist and political commentator. From 1877 to 1883, he worked as an editor for the conservative newspaper *Timpul* ("The Time"), where he published over 300 articles on politics, culture, and social issues. His writings often criticized the corruption and superficiality of Romanian society, advocating for a return to traditional values and a deeper engagement with national identity. Despite his literary success, Eminescu struggled with financial instability and poor health. In 1883, at the age of 33, he suffered a mental breakdown, likely exacerbated by syphilis, which had been diagnosed earlier. He was institutionalized for the first time in 1883 at the Dr. Șuțu Sanatorium in Bucharest, where he received treatment for what was then described as "nervous exhaustion."

Eminescu’s later years were marked by declining health and periods of institutionalization. He spent time in various sanatoriums, including the Ober-Döbling Clinic in Vienna (1886–1887) and the Mănăstirea Neamț monastery in Romania (1888–1889), where he sought solace in religion and nature. Despite his illness, he continued to write sporadically, producing some of his most poignant works, such as *"Glossă"* ("Gloss," 1883), a reflection on the fleeting nature of life. His final years were spent in Bucharest, where he lived in poverty, cared for by his sister Henrieta and a small circle of friends. On June 15, 1889, at the age of 39, Mihai Eminescu died in the Dr. Șuțu Sanatorium from complications related to syphilis and malnutrition. He was buried in the Bellu Cemetery in Bucharest, where his grave remains a site of pilgrimage for admirers of his work.

Eminescu’s legacy endures as a cornerstone of Romanian literature. His works have been translated into over 60 languages, and he is celebrated as a symbol of national identity and cultural pride. In 1948, the Romanian Academy posthumously elected him as a member, and in 2004, he was voted the "greatest Romanian" in a national poll. His influence extends beyond literature, shaping Romanian music, art, and philosophy, and his birthday, January 15, is observed as National Culture Day in Romania. Despite his tragically short life, Eminescu’s contributions to Romanian culture remain unparalleled, securing his place as one of Europe’s most important Romantic poets.
